title: Ali Usman Takes Maiden Five-For but Rues Pakistan's Bowling and Fielding Lapses at Headingley
excerpt: The left-arm spinner becomes the first visiting spinner to take five wickets at Headingley since 1972, but Pakistan's indisciplined seam attack and dropped catches hand England a 195-run lead.
body:
• Ali Usman claimed 5-92 at Headingley — his maiden Test five-wicket haul and the first by a visiting spinner at the ground since 1972.
  • Despite Usman's individual milestone, Pakistan's seamers bowled poorly and the fielding was abject, including a costly dropped catch of Harry Brook on one.
  • England closed Day 2 on 366-8 for a 195-run first-innings lead after four batters scored half-centuries.
  • Usman said he was proud of his five-for but lamented the lack of discipline across Pakistan's bowling and fielding units.

A Milestone Amid the Wreckage

Ali Usman's maiden Test five-wicket haul at Headingley was a personal triumph wedged inside a collective disaster. The 24-year-old left-arm spinner finished with 5-92 on Day 2 of the first Test, becoming the first visiting spinner to take five wickets at the ground since Australia's Ashley Mallett during the 1972 Ashes. But his achievement came against a backdrop of wayward seam bowling and dreadful fielding that allowed England to build a commanding 195-run first-innings lead.

Usman expressed mixed emotions after play, acknowledging pride in his personal landmark but ruing the lapses that undermined Pakistan's position.

How Usman Dismantled England's Middle Order

After Pakistan were bowled out for a meager 171 on Day 1, the onus was on the bowlers to keep the deficit manageable. Usman delivered where his seam colleagues could not. He found turn and variation on a Headingley pitch offering something for everyone, and his wickets came in a telling cluster.

His key scalp was Harry Brook, the world's top-ranked Test batter, who had made 91 from 93 balls when Usman's arm-ball skidded through his defences. It ended Brook's pursuit of a home-ground century for the second consecutive Headingley Test — he had been dismissed for 99 against India last summer.

Before Brook fell, Usman had dismissed Jordan Cox for 73, the debutant number three caught behind after misjudging the length of a full delivery. He then sealed his five-for with successive dismissals of Gus Atkinson, trapped lbw by one that straightened, and Ollie Robinson, who went first ball.

Indiscipline Elsewhere

Usman's excellence, however, was Pakistan's only redeeming feature on a bruising day. The seam attack, led by Mohammad Abbas and Khurram Shahzad, offered occasional menace but lacked the consistency to build sustained pressure. After a rain-delayed resumption, Khurram's first ball hooped dangerously past Joe Root's outside edge — but his third over leaked 17 runs, including four boundaries. Four-balls were two-a-penny.

The fielding was worse. Brook was dropped on just one at second slip by stand-in captain Salman Ali Agha off Khurram Shahzad, a regulation chance that cost Pakistan dearly. Brook went on to score 90 more runs, sharing a 120-run partnership with Dan Lawrence that killed the contest.

"Pakistan's abject fielding standards leave no place to hide. On a tough day in the field, the visitors made it tougher still by having no discipline in the one discipline they control."

— Danyal Rasool, ESPNcricinfo

Root made 66, Cox 73, Lawrence 51, and Brook 91 — four half-centuries that each punished Pakistan's looseness. England scored at 4.46 runs per over, matching the run rate of the previous Stokes-McCullum "Bazball" era, but without needing to take any risks. The runs simply came from Pakistan's errors.

Pakistan Stare Down the Barrel

England closed on 366-8 with two wickets still in hand, a lead of 195 that looks unassailable given how their bowlers dismantled Pakistan's batting on Day 1. With better weather forecast for the remaining three days and the pitch offering assistance to both seam and spin, Pakistan face the near-impossible task of batting out of trouble against an attack featuring Robinson (5-51 on Day 1) and Josh Tongue (5-46).

For Usman, the five-wicket haul will be a career-defining moment — proof of his ability to compete in English conditions where left-arm spin rarely thrives. But personal milestones matter little when the team is staring at a heavy defeat. Pakistan last won a Test in England eight years ago, and nothing from the first two days at Headingley suggests that drought is about to end.
